section.para: This envelope satisfies both subscriptions, because it contains an item of each subscribed class. The ONVIF Device therefore delivers it on subscription 31 as well, as a separate occurrence with its own eventId. The data field is abridged below: it carries the envelope shown above, byte for byte, and only its identifier is repeated here so that the two deliveries can be seen to refer to one envelope.

The empty items list above is an artefact of the abridgement and never appears on the wire: items is mandatory and carries at least one item, and here it carries the two items delivered on subscription 30.

The ONVIF Client now holds the same two items twice, under two different eventId values. It deduplicates on the item identifiers 6b1e0d92-… and 9f4c2a61-…, not on eventId, which is per-delivery and differs precisely because the delivery differed. Item identifiers are unique and never reused, which makes this deduplication exact.

The correspondences between the MCP occurrence and the ONVIF envelope are worth reading off this example, since the two levels are easy to confuse (see ). The name VehicleObservation and the @type of the item happen to be the same string, but they are different fields serving different purposes: the first says which subscription this delivery belongs to, the second says what the item is. The eventId evt_veh_0002 is not the identifier of the envelope 5d3b8e07-…, nor of any item in it. The timestamp 13:05:04.310Z is when the device dispatched the occurrence, and is not the productionTime of either item, still less the observedTime of 13:05:04.000Z. And cursor is a position in the subscription, not a fact about the world: it is the one field an ONVIF Client persists and sends back, and it carries no evidential weight.

Every line of an SSE event carries its own data: prefix. This is not a typographical device of this document but the framing rule of text/event-stream: the prefix is a field name, not part of the payload, and a receiver strips it from each line and joins the remainders with a line feed to recover the payload. A JSON document may therefore be laid out over as many lines as readability calls for — the line feeds reintroduced by the receiver are insignificant whitespace between JSON tokens, and a payload can never contain a raw line feed of its own because JSON escapes them inside strings. An implementation MAY equally emit each notification on a single data: line; the two forms are indistinguishable to the receiver. A blank line terminates the event.

The keep-alive frame is sent once per keep-alive interval, whatever interval is in force on the stream, when that stream delivered no event during the interval. See for how the ONVIF Client changes that interval.

Neither envelope above carries a signature. Signing is optional, and on a continuous metadata stream a device may reasonably omit it; the price is that the items carry no integrity or non-repudiation claim. shows the signed form.

section.title: How the second event refines the first
section.para: The two events above are the normal way in which analytics improves its own output, and the model is built so that it can do so without ever contradicting itself. It is worth following what each of the three items claims.

At 13:05:00 the device saw something at the main gate. It was confident enough that a vehicle was there to report it — a confidence of 0.62 — but it could determine neither the type of the vehicle nor the use it was being put to. Both fields carry Unknown. This is not a defect of the report: type is a mandatory slot, and Unknown is what allows the device to state a detection it is sure of without inventing a classification it is not. Had the device not classified vehicle use at all, the use field would have been absent rather than Unknown; here it is present and Unknown, which says something more specific — the device does classify use, and it tried, and it failed. An ONVIF Client can tell those two situations apart, and they call for different responses.

At 13:05:04 the same device, on the same channel, saw a vehicle at the ambulance drop-off and this time classified it: a Van in Ambulance use, at a confidence of 0.94. Nothing in this second observation refers to the first. It is an independent report of what the sensor saw at a different place and a different time, and it would be exactly the same report if the first observation had never been made.

The link between the two is the third item, and it is a different kind of claim altogether. VehicleReidentification is an Assessment: it states that observations 2c9f4b18-… and 6b1e0d92-… are of the same physical vehicle. It lists both in supportedBy, which is why that field requires at least two entries — a single observation cannot be re-identified. It assigns the vehicle a stable identifier, vehicleId c4d81f36-…, which designates the physical vehicle and not any information item, and which a later re-identification of the same vehicle will reuse, so that an ONVIF Client can accumulate what is known about one vehicle over time. And it nominates 6b1e0d92-… as the authoritativeObservation, telling the client which of the two classifications to prefer.

What the assessment does not do is modify either observation. The item 2c9f4b18-… still says Unknown, still at a confidence of 0.62, and it will say so for as long as it is retained. Nothing is retracted, nothing is overwritten, and an ONVIF Client that received the first event and then lost its connection is not holding a report that has since become false — it is holding a true report of what the sensor could determine at 13:05:00. An Observation is never revised, and this is the property that makes a metadata stream auditable: an observation recorded at the time of an incident reads afterwards exactly as it read then. What changes is not the record but what can be concluded from it, and conclusions are separate items with their own identity.

The provenances make the distinction visible. Both observations are provenanced to an ONVIFDevice naming the video source that produced them. The assessment is provenanced to an AnalyticsModule — token ReID_1, algorithm vehicle-reidentification, version 4.2.0 — because an algorithm, not a sensor, produced it. The two items travel in the same envelope and leave the device through the same interface, but they do not have the same author, and an ONVIF Client may have good reason to accept what the sensor reports while treating the re-identification with more caution, or to accept re-identifications from version 4.2.0 of this algorithm and not from an earlier one. That decision is only available to a client if the items say who made them, which is why provenance is mandatory and why the two concrete provenance classes are distinct.

Confidence follows the same rule. The assessment is at 0.88 while the observation it nominates as authoritative is at 0.94, and this ordering is the expected one: the algorithm is at least as uncertain as its evidence, since it may have matched the wrong vehicle even where each individual observation was sound. An ONVIF Client shall not propagate the confidence of an observation to an assessment that cites it, in either direction.

Finally, the two observations reached the client in two separate envelopes, four seconds apart, while the assessment travelled together with the observation it was derived from. That is the general pattern: items whose production is separated in time are not gathered into one envelope but linked by identifier, whereas an assessment and the observation produced at the same moment are delivered together, so that a client receives the claim and its immediate support in one delivery. The reference to 2c9f4b18-… resolves against what the client already holds; if it does not — because the client subscribed too late, or applied a filter that excluded the first observation — then the client holds an assessment it cannot fully resolve, and shall treat it as such rather than discarding the envelope.

section.title: Webhook delivery of the same events
section.para: Webhook subscription request (Client to Device): Instead of keeping a stream open, the ONVIF Client MAY register a callback URL for the same event type, when the device advertises "webhook" in delivery.

Webhook delivery (Device to callback endpoint): As matching events occur, the ONVIF Device POSTs each EventOccurrence to the registered callback URL, signed per Standard Webhooks and identifying the subscription. The occurrence is the same object that the stream carried, and the payload is the same InformationEnvelope; only the framing differs.

The webhook signature attests the transport: it tells the callback endpoint that this HTTP request came from the party holding the subscription secret. It says nothing about the items inside, and it does not survive the request — once the body has been read, the signature is gone. An envelope that has to remain verifiable after delivery carries its own signature, as shown in ; the two mechanisms protect different things and neither substitutes for the other.

section.title: Signed information envelope example
section.para: The example below shows a complete InformationEnvelope signed with the OnvifSignature profile defined in . It encloses two observations produced by the same channel: a vehicle observation and the observation of its licence plate.

Two details are worth noting. First, the entries of hashes are not in the order in which the items were produced: the licence plate observation was produced second but appears first, because its identifier sorts before the one of the vehicle observation. This is the ordering rule of at work. Second, the key field uses a PublicKeyIdentifier, so the certificate chain is not repeated in the envelope.

The provenance of both items is a concrete Provenance subclass describing a device (see ) with its descriptive fields populated and the channel named, so that the example reads clearly. All of those fields are optional, and the minimal form of the class — a single key identifier — is equally valid and considerably shorter, which matters because provenance is repeated on every item. The stream examples of use that minimal form.

Here the declared key carries a fingerprint as well as an identifier (see ), and the same fingerprint appears in the key field of the signature. Three things can therefore be checked, and they are not the same check. The keyId declared in publicKeys equals the one the signature names, so the envelope was signed with a key the producing device claims as its own. The fingerprints equal each other, so the two references are to the same key material and not merely to the same keystore entry name. And an ONVIF Client that obtained this device's key fingerprint through the Advanced Security Service, or at provisioning, can compare it with the value here and establish that the key is the one it trusts — which no comparison internal to the envelope could establish, since an attacker who fabricates an envelope can make it internally consistent.

The fingerprint in the key field is covered by the signature, because key is part of the signature configuration and the configuration is hashed into envelopeDigest. The fingerprints in publicKeys are covered by the per-item digests, since provenance is part of the content of an item. Neither can be substituted without invalidating something.

The signatureValue above is abridged, as are the certificates later in this section: a DER encoded ECDSA P-256 signature is 96 base64 characters and does not fit the width of this page. The trailing ellipsis marks the elision and is not part of the value, which on the wire is base64 characters and padding alone, with nothing else inside the string. Every digest in the example is shown in full, since a SHA-256 digest fits.

In this example envelopeDigest is obtained by hashing the canonical form of the signature configuration — that is, the signature object above without envelopeDigest and signatureValue — followed by the raw octets of the two digests, taken in the order in which they appear in hashes. The base64 text of the digests is not what is concatenated; the bytes it encodes are.

When the certificate chain has to travel with the envelope, the key field carries an X509CertificateChain instead. The chain is ordered from the leaf certificate outwards and stops short of the certification authority certificate:
Because key is part of the signature configuration, changing the key descriptor — including switching between these two forms — changes envelopeDigest and therefore requires a new signature.

section.title: Dynamic schema re-registration
section.para: This example shows the recovery procedure of . The device has been updated and now emits a vendor class, acme:ThermalObservation, which the ONVIF Client does not hold: the prefix acme is bound by no module the client loaded when it established the session. The inline context binds the acme prefix, but the client does not yet hold a module declaring the expanded class URI; that unresolved class is the trigger.

Event notification with an unresolvable type (Device to Client): the notification is delivered on the open events/stream response. The envelope carries two items, only one of which the client can interpret.

The suspended item is then validated, and every subsequent item of the class is validated as it arrives.

This path is a recovery path, not the normal one. The ONVIF Device should have announced the change with notifications/events/list_changed, on receipt of which the client would have re-called events/list and resources/list and loaded the module before the first item of the new class was ever delivered. The procedure above is what keeps the client working when that announcement did not arrive, or arrived too late.

appendix.title: Wire Format Example — November 2026 Hackathon (informative)
appendix.para: This annex is informative, and its validity is limited to the duration of the ONVIF hackathon held in Mexico City in November 2026. It is not part of the specification of the Agentic Service and shall not be relied upon after that event.

The payloads below use the classes of the hackathon module hackathon.yaml, namespace https://www.onvif.org/ver10/agentic/hackathon-2026.11/linkml/, alongside the classes of the ONVIF Agentic Schema Bundle. The hackathon module is served as a resource by the participating devices in the same way as any other module, and it is deleted when the event is over: a class named here is not a class of this specification, and no future revision is bound by it.

The scenario is a straight road watched by two cameras placed two hundred metres apart. Each camera reports a vehicle detection carrying the licence plate it read. An analytics box derives an average speed from the two detections and publishes it together with a collection that groups the three observations. A service running on a server compares that speed with the limit in force and issues a speeding assessment. Four parties therefore produce information, and each one signs an envelope of its own.
The identifiers are fixed throughout this annex so that the references between the items can be followed:

Every payload below is a complete InformationEnvelope and validates against the bundle together with the hackathon module. The digests and signature values are well-formed base64 of the right length but are not real: they were not computed over these payloads, and a participant reproducing this annex shall compute its own by the procedure of .

The inline context of each envelope binds both onvif and hackathon2026. It also defines type-scoped contexts for the hackathon classes that declare attributes of their own. Consequently every @type expands to the class URI assigned by its LinkML module, while an unqualified property such as algorithm expands according to the class on which it occurs and cannot be confused with an ONVIF property having the same JSON spelling.

section.title: Entry camera
section.para: The vehicle passes the first camera at 10:15:00.000 UTC. The camera reads the plate and emits one VehicleDetectionObservation in an envelope it signs with its own key.

The featureOfInterest and the procedure carry the values the class fixes, Vehicle and Analytics, as specified in : an ONVIF Client knows both from the class of the item and does not have to read them. The observedTime is the instant the vehicle was seen and the productionTime is the later instant at which the item was assembled; the speed is computed from the first and never from the second.

The key that signed the envelope, cam-entry-signing-1, is the same key the provenance declares in publicKeys. The two identifiers are drawn from the same keystore identifier space, as specified in , so an ONVIF Client can establish that the envelope was signed with a key the producing device claims as its own, and can look that key up through the Advanced Security Service.

section.title: Exit camera
section.para: The same vehicle passes the second camera ten seconds later, at 10:15:10.000 UTC. The item has the same shape as the one above and differs in what was observed and in who observed it.

The two cameras are separate devices here, so what distinguishes the two detections is the provenance itself: a different serialNumber and a different signing key. Were the two cameras channels of one device, the provenance would name the same device twice and the entity field would be what told the two video sources apart.

The two detections carry the same plate, and that is the whole of what ties them to one vehicle in this use case. The claim that the two are the same vehicle is not made by either camera: it is made by the analytics box in the next section, and it is made by the act of computing a speed from the pair.

section.title: Analytics box
section.para: The analytics box has received the two envelopes above and has verified them. It matches the two detections by plate, orders them by observedTime, takes the distance between the two observedSpace values and the difference of the two instants, and obtains two hundred metres in ten seconds, which is 72.0 km/h.

It publishes two information items in one envelope of its own. The first is the SpeedEstimateObservation it computed, which cites the two detections in supportedBy. The second is an ObservationsCollection that groups the three observations, so that a later item can cite one identifier instead of three.

The two detections are not repeated here. A collection carries identifiers and not observations, as specified in , and each identifier resolves to an observation the ONVIF Client has already received — in this case from the two envelopes of the previous sections, each signed by the camera that produced it. Nothing would be gained by the box re-publishing them: an item does not carry a signature of its own, so a detection copied into this envelope would be covered by the signature of the box and would no longer be evidence of what the camera said.
Three details of this envelope are worth reading closely.

The provenance of both items is an AnalyticsModule and not an ONVIFDevice, because an algorithm produced them: the box did not look at the road. Its version is what makes the estimate reproducible, since a change in the computation changes the speed without changing either detection.

The procedure carries a custom URI and no onvif value, because ProcedureType names no two-point transit computation. This is the extension branch of an open vocabulary, as specified in , and the URI is in the namespace of the hackathon.

The two entries of hashes are sorted by their item field and not by the order of the items in the envelope: the collection precedes the estimate here, while in items the estimate comes first. The ordering of hashes is normative, for the reason given in .

The confidence of the collection is 1.0. A collection states nothing about the physical world that its members do not state, so there is nothing for a confidence to qualify; the field is inherited from InformationItem and is mandatory there, and 1.0 is the only value that adds no claim of its own.

section.title: Assessment service on the server
section.para: The service on the server has received the envelope of the analytics box and verified it. It reads the speed, compares it with the limit of 50.0 km/h in force on that road, allows a tolerance of 3.0 km/h, finds 72.0 above 53.0, and issues one SpeedingAssessment.

The assessment cites the ObservationsCollection in supportedBy, and that one identifier is what a collection is for: it stands for the speed estimate and the two detections at once, and an ONVIF Client that resolves it reaches all three. The assessment restates the measured speed, the limit and the plate on its own result, so that it can be read and acted upon without any reference being resolved.

The item is an Assessment and not an Observation because the limit is not contained in anything the cameras or the box measured: it comes from a provision in force at that place, and the same speed yields an assessment on one road and none on another. No assessment is emitted where the limit was respected, so the existence of this item is itself the statement that it was exceeded, as specified in .

The provenance is a SoftwareService and not an ONVIFDevice: the party that issues the fine is not the party that watched the road, and an ONVIF Client shall be able to tell the two apart. The service is not obliged to hold a keystore, which is why its publicKeys field is optional; this one does hold keys and declares them, so the same comparison between the signing key and the declared key that was made for the entry camera can be made here.

An ONVIF Client that has received all four envelopes holds a chain it can walk backwards without trusting any single party twice: the assessment names the collection, the collection names the estimate and the two detections, the estimate names the two detections, and each of the four envelopes carries a signature made with a key the producer of its items declares as its own. Each link is a reference to an identifier, and the acyclicity and productionTime ordering of the chain hold throughout, as specified in .

section.title: Driving the assessment service — configure, start and stop
section.para: The envelope of the preceding section is the output of a function execution, and this section shows the three calls that bring that execution about: the criterion is configured once, an execution is started, and the execution is stopped when it is no longer wanted. The party that exposes the Agentic Service endpoint plays the role this specification calls the ONVIF Device, whether it is a camera or, as here, a service running on a server; the ONVIF Client is the console of the traffic authority. The four classes exercised below — SpeedingAssessmentConfig, SpeedingAssessmentCapabilities, SpeedingAssessmentExecutionParameters and SpeedingAssessmentExecutionResult — belong to the hackathon module, not to this specification. The module binds the four to the function name with a fifth class, SpeedingAssessmentInvocation, a specialization of FunctionInvocation as required by ; that class is a declaration and appears in no payload below.
Request (Client to Device): The ONVIF Client calls list_functions first, as required by , because it needs the local name to call and the schema URIs that govern what it may send.
Response (Device to Client): The service supports one function of its own, plus the function this specification reserves.

The canonicalUri of speeding_assessment lies in the hackathon namespace and not in https://www.onvif.org/ver10/agentic/function/, which is reserved to the functions this specification defines, as set out in . The entry is listed with enabled: false: the function exists on this instance but no criterion has been applied to it yet, so the client can see that speeding assessments are obtainable here and knows that configure_function has to come first.
Request (Client to Device): The client reads the capabilities before configuring, so that it learns the bounds rather than discovering them through a rejected configuration.

Response (Device to Client): The capabilities object is an instance of SpeedingAssessmentCapabilities, the class named in capabilitiesSchema above. These values are invariant for this instance: they are the same before and after any execution.
Request (Client to Device): The config object is an instance of SpeedingAssessmentConfig, the class named in configSchema, and the client validates it against the compiled schema before sending it.
Response (Device to Client): The device confirms the applied configuration and does not start the function.

These five values are the criterion, and they are configured rather than passed per execution for a reason that can be read off the assessment of : that item restates speedLimit 50.0, tolerance 3.0 and the same rule on its own result, so a client can check the claim against the configuration that produced it. A criterion that changed from one execution to the next could not be stated that way, and two assessments of the same service would not be comparable. minimumConfidence is the lowest confidence a SpeedEstimateObservation may carry to be assessed at all: the estimate of the analytics box carries 0.9 and is above it, and an estimate below 0.75 would be ignored rather than assessed, since a fine cannot rest on a measurement its own producer does not stand behind. emitOnlyWhenExceeded is left at its default of true, which is what makes the mere existence of an assessment the statement that the limit was exceeded.
Request (Client to Device): The function is now configured, so it can be started. The parameters object is an instance of SpeedingAssessmentExecutionParameters, the class named in executionSchema.
Response (Device to Client): The structuredContent is an instance of SpeedingAssessmentExecutionResult, the class named in resultSchema.

The response reports the start of the execution and nothing about its outcome. Where starting is asynchronous the device may return a task instead, in the form shown in ; that task represents the start alone and reaches a terminal state once the execution is running, rather than staying working for as long as the function is active. The assessments themselves arrive afterwards as metadata events, each in a signed envelope of its own: the envelope of is one of them, produced at 10:15:12 by this execution. validity bears on the run and not on the criterion, which is why it is an execution parameter; where it is omitted the execution runs until it is stopped. dryRun is false here, so the assessments are real; with true the service would evaluate the same criterion and report what it would have produced without emitting any SpeedingAssessment, which is how a limit can be tried against live traffic before any fine follows from it. The client may ask for a dry run only because supportsDryRun was true in the capabilities.

Request (Client to Device): The shift ends early and the execution is stopped before its validity expires. stop_function takes the execution identifier the start returned, and no per-function parameters: stopping needs none, which is why the hackathon module declares no class for it.

Response (Device to Client): No field of the descriptor names a class for the result of a stop, so the device reports the outcome in the textual content and the absence of an error is the confirmation.

Stopping the execution ends the emission of assessments; it does not withdraw the ones already emitted, nor does it discard the configuration. The criterion stays applied, so the client can start a further execution over another interval without configuring again, and the entry would now be listed with enabled: true. Nothing in this exchange touches the envelopes of the preceding sections: an assessment already published remains verifiable after the execution that produced it is over, because what carries the signature is the envelope it was delivered in and what binds the signature to that one item is its own digest, as specified in .
